title: Quiz: Floating Point Instructions - Fundamentals
prompt: Test your ability to work with single and double-precision floating-point registers, type conversions, and FPU arithmetic instructions.

questions.question: How many bits are used by the 'D' registers to hold double-precision floating-point numbers?
questions.explanation: D registers use the low-order 64 bits of the 128-bit FP registers to hold double-precision floating-point numbers. S registers use the low-order 32 bits for single-precision.
questions.hint: The 'D' stands for Double, which is twice the size of a 32-bit single-precision float.

questions.question: Which prefix must be used in an assembly pseudo-op to correctly specify a 'real' floating-point value?
questions.explanation: You must use the prefix '0r' to specify a 'real' floating-point value when initializing memory using `.single` or `.double` pseudo-ops.

questions.question: If an assembly subroutine returns a double-precision floating-point number to the calling C function, which register will contain the return value?
questions.explanation: A double-precision FP number is returned from a subroutine in register d0. A single-precision value is returned in s0.
questions.hint: It uses the lowest-numbered register corresponding to the double-precision size.

questions.question: How do basic floating-point arithmetic instructions (like `fadd` and `fmul`) differ from integer arithmetic instructions regarding operands?
options: They use registers only and do not allow immediate values.
They require a memory address as the third operand.
They automatically update the condition flags without needing a special suffix.
questions.explanation: Basic floating-point arithmetic instructions use registers only; they do not accept immediate values.
questions.hint: You must load your floating-point constants into registers before doing math with them.

questions.question: When debugging in GDB, which command format is used to print the contents of a floating-point register?
questions.explanation: In gdb, you use `p/f` to print the contents of a floating-point register (e.g., `p/f $d0`).
questions.hint: The format specifier is the first letter of 'float'.
